title: How he compiled
hook: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi, side by side with the Gurus: how Guru Arjan chose what went into the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan sang that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other, and serves the One alone. Your line was serving the one.

A stack of handwritten pages, gathered from many hands. Some hold the Gurus' hymns, copied and recopied in different towns, a word drifting here and there. Some hold songs by saints who were never Gurus: a weaver, a man who worked with hides, a Sufi from the Punjab. And tradition says some pages going around carried the Guru's name without the Guru's voice. Somebody has to sit with all of it and decide what goes into one book, and what stays out. Today, Guru Arjan is the editor.
screen: `A STACK OF PAGES, MANY HANDS.` → `SAINTS WHO WERE NEVER GURUS.` → `WHAT GOES IN, WHAT STAYS OUT?`

segments.voice: You've met the scribe, Bhai Gurdas, and the Gurus answering Farid; today, the editor's test. Tradition says Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and dictated the volume to Bhai Gurdas, who wrote it out. The book became the Adi Granth, which later became the Guru Granth Sahib. So what was his test? Not where a singer was born, which faith he grew up in, or whether his trade was respected. The test was whether the hymn agreed with the Guru's teaching: the One, the Name, the turning away from ego. Look who passed. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his own verses. Ravidas names his people's work with hides and dead cattle, work his society looked down on, and sings that the learned now bow to him because of the Name. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, has his saloks near the end of the Granth. These aren't footnotes; they're sung in the gurdwara, in the same ragas as the Gurus' hymns. And among Farid's saloks, a few verses are marked Mahala three and Mahala five: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, answering. Where one of Farid's lines could be heard too harshly, a Guru's line sits beside it, turning it a little. So choosing carefully meant a wide welcome and a real conversation. The Guru didn't flatten the voices into one. He let them sing, and he answered. His question wasn't, is this person like me? It was, does this agree with the truth?
screen: `THE GURU DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `THE TEST: DOES IT AGREE?` · `A WEAVER, A LEATHERWORKER, A SUFI.` · `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID.` · then, large: `HE CHOSE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Let the voices of your week pass by, a podcast, a parent, a teacher, a song, a friend's text, without judging them yet. Then ask the editor's question of each: does this agree with the person I'm trying to become? Keep the one that stands out, maybe from somewhere you didn't expect, and hold one thing it said.
How he compiled. Guru Arjan gathered many voices, Gurus and saints, and kept the ones that agreed with the Guru's teaching, whoever sang them. Today's word.
Your line: he chose carefully. A wide welcome, and one test. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, the hymns of the Gurus and of the bhagats, such as Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid, are read and sung from the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bow to the whole as the Guru.

put it in, and sing it with the Gurus' hymns.
keep it in a separate book of extras.

chat.says: Why are a weaver and a Sufi in the Sikh scripture, if they weren't Gurus?
options: Guru Arjan's test was whether a hymn agreed with the teaching, not who sang it.
They were added later by scribes, without the Guru ever knowing about it.
They're kept at the back as footnotes, and never sung in the gurdwara.
chat.meaning: Tradition says Guru Arjan kept hymns that agreed with the Guru's teaching, whoever sang them. Kabir, Ravidas and Farid are sung in the same ragas.

Bhai Gurdas.meaning: the learned Sikh who wrote out the volume, tradition says

Adi Granth.meaning: the first volume of the scripture, Guru Arjan's compilation

Kabir.meaning: a weaver-poet whose hymns are in the Granth

Ravidas.meaning: a poet-saint whose people worked with hides

Sheikh Farid.meaning: a Sufi of the Punjab, with saloks in the Granth

Mahala.meaning: the heading that marks which Guru is speaking
